newsitem.title: FRANCE: Wheat importers fold arms and wait as prices tumble.
newsitem.headline: Wheat importers fold arms and wait as prices tumble.

text.p: Sliding world wheat prices have failed to spark serious buying by importing nations, leaving markets looking shaky as harvest time approaches in the northern hemisphere, European grain traders said on Wednesday.
Benchmark July Chicago wheat futures fell three percent on Tuesday to $3.63-1/2 a bushel after funds dumped the contract on improved crop chances following rain in the United States.

Wheat has fallen steadily from a recent peak near $4.50 a bushel hit on fears of frost damage that later receded. Some analysts see room for a fall towards $3.50, though technical charts suggest a few upward blips on the way.
"There is little demand right now and many buyers are covered through July. They are not in a hurry," one trader said.
The latest prices translate into wheat offered on the world market between $135 and $140 a tonne, far below the records of almost twice that seen in April last year when stocks were low.
European exporters have been mostly squeezed off the world market by a wait-and-see policy on the next harvest by the European Commission, which has imposed taxes to throttle sales.
But exporters said current prices in the United States and elsewhere were "very interesting" to importers, many of whom were checking prices but biding their time before buying.
Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia were among countries said to be watching from the market's fringes without putting in buying orders.

Egypt is the sole major importer to have bought wheat in any quantity recently, though at somewhat higher prices, while a record Iranian buying spree seems to have paused for now. Eastern Europe looks set to recover from poor crops last year.

Despite the European slowdown, traders cited ample supplies leaving Canadian ports, the expected arrival of the new U.S. wheat crop in several weeks and a couple of million tonnes left to sell from Australia's bumper crop to reach a 20 million tonne goal.
Unlike last year when importers competed for every last bushel in store right up to the new harvest, most seem happy to wait out the gap between crop cycles and watch prices crumple.
"There is more surplus around generally and buyers are feeling more comfortable," a European trader said.
A big factor driving wheat downwards has been a bail-out of speculative positions built up on reports of significant damage to the U.S. hard red winter crop when a freeze hit in April.

"In fact weather conditions since the freeze have been nothing short of ideal, leaving the market wondering how much damage will actually be evident when final yields come in," London-based brokerage GNI Ltd said in a commodity market note.

France, which dominates European output, is recovering from a late winter drought, fuelling hopes of a crop very near last year's record of 34 million tonnes. That will likely put pressure on Brussels to resume export subsidies in the face of U.S. opposition this year, to maintain its number three ranking on the world market behind the United States and Canada.

Some traders cautioned wheat would snap higher if importers come out in a block to buy as prices stabilise. But most expect the market will find it harder to rally unless the weather really turns foul and the days of huge buying by Russia and China remain buried by financial woes or good Chinese crops.
